messages.content: customers say one of our trailer MP4s starts really slow on mobile data but is fine once it plays. how do I confirm the moov atom is at the end of that file, and what remux fixes it?

content.text: I'll look up the faststart guidance in the knowledge base.

input.query: moov atom at end of file faststart slow start progressive MP4 remux

content.content:
{"results": [{"id": "mp4-faststart", "title": "Progressive MP4 takes long to start (moov atom at the end)", "text": "# Progressive MP4 takes long to start (moov atom at the end)

An MP4 file's index (the `moov` atom) is often written at the end of the file by recorders and
encoders. A progressive-download player must then fetch the end of the file before playback can
begin, which shows up as a long start delay or extra range requests.

Checks and fix:
- `ffprobe -v trace file.mp4 2>&1 | grep -m2 -E "type:'(moov|mdat)'"` shows which atom comes first.
- Remux with the index at the front: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c copy -movflags +faststart out.mp4`.
- For adaptive streaming, prefer fragmented MP4 (DASH or HLS) instead."}, {"id": "av-sync", "title": "Audio and video drift out of sync", "text": "# Audio and video drift out of sync

Players normally treat the audio clock as the master and schedule video frames against it.
Drift usually comes from wrong timestamps rather than from rendering speed.

Checks:
- Inspect stream start times and timestamps with `ffprobe -show_streams -show_frames`; a large
  `start_time` difference between audio and video streams shows up as constant offset.
- Variable-frame-rate recordings (common from phone cameras) can drift when a pipeline assumes
  a constant frame rate. Remux or transcode with correct timestamps.
- When writing a custom renderer, use `AudioTrack.getTimestamp()` to map audio frames to
  real time instead of counting written bytes."}, {"id": "av1-decoding", "title": "AV1 decoding support on Android", "text": "# AV1 decoding support on Android

Android ships a software AV1 decoder (`c2.android.av1.decoder`) starting with Android 10
(API 29). Hardware AV1 decoding depends on the device's SoC, not on the Android version: many
devices on recent Android releases still decode AV1 in software only, which can be too slow
for high resolutions or frame rates.

Checks:
- Enumerate `MediaCodecList(MediaCodecList.REGULAR_CODECS)` for the MIME type `video/av01`.
- On API 29+, `MediaCodecInfo.isHardwareAccelerated()` tells you whether a decoder is
  hardware backed.
- Use `CodecCapabilities.getVideoCapabilities()` to check supported sizes and frame rates
  before choosing an AV1 rendition; fall back to VP9 or H.264/HEVC when needed."}]}

messages.content: A customer's live channel dies after their app sits in background, and the log they sent has a live window error near the bottom. What should I check first to tell whether this is a player setting or a stream timing issue?

content.text: I'll check the knowledge base on this live window error.

input.query: BehindLiveWindowException live window background player setting stream timing

content.content:
{"results": [{"id": "behind-live-window", "title": "BehindLiveWindowException in Media3 / ExoPlayer live streams", "text": "# BehindLiveWindowException in Media3 / ExoPlayer live streams

A live stream exposes a sliding window of segments. If playback falls further behind than
the window (long pause, slow network, app in the background), the segments it needs are gone
and the player raises a `BehindLiveWindowException`, surfaced as a `PlaybackException` with
error code `ERROR_CODE_BEHIND_LIVE_WINDOW`.

Fix: in `Player.Listener.onPlayerError`, check for that error code, then call
`player.seekToDefaultPosition()` followed by `player.prepare()` to rejoin at the live edge.
Consider a longer live window on the server or a smaller target live offset on the client."}, {"id": "audio-focus", "title": "Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)", "text": "# Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)

Android coordinates audio between apps with audio focus. An app that never requests focus,
or ignores focus loss, keeps playing over navigation prompts, calls, or other media.

Fix:
- With Media3, pass suitable `AudioAttributes` and `handleAudioFocus = true` to
  `ExoPlayer.setAudioAttributes(...)`; the player then requests focus, ducks, and pauses for you.
- Without Media3, request focus with an `AudioFocusRequest` (API 26+) and react to
  `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS`, `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT`, and `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT_CAN_DUCK`.
- Also handle `ACTION_AUDIO_BECOMING_NOISY` to pause when headphones are unplugged."}]}

{"results": [{"id": "audio-focus", "title": "Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)", "text": "# Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)

Android coordinates audio between apps with audio focus. An app that never requests focus,
or ignores focus loss, keeps playing over navigation prompts, calls, or other media.

Fix:
- With Media3, pass suitable `AudioAttributes` and `handleAudioFocus = true` to
  `ExoPlayer.setAudioAttributes(...)`; the player then requests focus, ducks, and pauses for you.
- Without Media3, request focus with an `AudioFocusRequest` (API 26+) and react to
  `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS`, `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT`, and `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT_CAN_DUCK`.
- Also handle `ACTION_AUDIO_BECOMING_NOISY` to pause when headphones are unplugged."}, {"id": "av-sync", "title": "Audio and video drift out of sync", "text": "# Audio and video drift out of sync

Players normally treat the audio clock as the master and schedule video frames against it.
Drift usually comes from wrong timestamps rather than from rendering speed.

Checks:
- Inspect stream start times and timestamps with `ffprobe -show_streams -show_frames`; a large
  `start_time` difference between audio and video streams shows up as constant offset.
- Variable-frame-rate recordings (common from phone cameras) can drift when a pipeline assumes
  a constant frame rate. Remux or transcode with correct timestamps.
- When writing a custom renderer, use `AudioTrack.getTimestamp()` to map audio frames to
  real time instead of counting written bytes."}]}

content.text:
Likely cause: atlas-a1 reports two AV1 decoders: the hardware "c2.atlas.av1.decoder" ("hardware": true, Main and Main10, up to 3840x2160 at 60 fps) and the software "c2.android.av1.decoder" ("hardware": false, Main only, 20 fps at max size). av1_2160p60.mkv is AV1 Main at 3840x2160, 60/1 fps, so only the hardware decoder can meet its size and frame rate; the software one tops out at 20 fps. messages.content: On the HDR path we pass HDR10 static metadata through MediaFormat KEY_HDR_STATIC_INFO, but the decoder output still looks flat on the panel. Which of the colour transfer and mastering display fields should we check first to find where the metadata gets dropped?

content.text: I'll check the knowledge base on HDR metadata handling.

input.query: HDR10 KEY_HDR_STATIC_INFO KEY_COLOR_TRANSFER ST2084 mastering display metadata flat

content.content:
{"results": [{"id": "hdr-tone-mapping", "title": "HDR video looks washed out or too dark", "text": "# HDR video looks washed out or too dark

HDR10 and HLG streams carry a wide colour gamut (BT.2020) and a high-dynamic-range transfer
function (PQ or HLG). When such a stream reaches a display path that is not HDR-capable and
nothing tone-maps it, colours look flat and grey or the picture looks far too dark.

Checks:
- Ask the display what it supports: `Display.getHdrCapabilities()` (or `Display.isHdr()` on API 26+).
- Render to a `SurfaceView`. `TextureView` composites through the GPU and is a common reason
  HDR output gets flattened.
- Confirm the decoder output format reports the expected colour transfer
  (`MediaFormat.KEY_COLOR_TRANSFER`) and colour standard.
- If the display is SDR, tone-map explicitly (for example with a Media3 Transformer or
  effect pipeline) or serve an SDR rendition."}]}

messages.content: one of our test phones only gets SD on the DRM stream even on wifi, and it started after the new firmware went on. can you check whether the widevine security level is capping the resolution?

content.text: I'll check the device's DRM and decoder info. Please tell me the device id if it isn't lumen-l3.

input.query: Widevine security level resolution cap L3 SD firmware

content.content: {"android_api_level": 33, "decoders": [{"hardware": true, "max_fps_at_max_size": 60, "max_height": 1080, "max_width": 1920, "mime": "video/avc", "name": "c2.lumen.avc.decoder", "profiles": ["Baseline", "Main", "High"]}], "device": "lumen-l3", "display_hdr_types": [], "max_concurrent_hw_video_decoders": 4, "mime": "video/avc", "widevine_security_level": "L3"}

{"results": [{"id": "widevine-levels", "title": "Widevine security levels and HD playback", "text": "# Widevine security levels and HD playback

Widevine has security levels: L1 (decryption and decoding inside a hardware trusted
environment) and L3 (software only). Content owners commonly restrict HD and higher
renditions to L1, so the same app may get only SD on an L3 device.

Checks:
- Read `MediaDrm(WIDEVINE_UUID).getPropertyString("securityLevel")`.
- A device can drop from L1 to L3 after an unlocked bootloader or a failed keybox
  provisioning; the license server then refuses HD keys.
- Log the license request and response status to tell a policy refusal apart from a
  network or provisioning error."}, {"id": "mediacodec-errors", "title": "MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures", "text": "# MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures

`MediaCodec.CodecException` reports whether an error is transient (`isTransient()`: retry the
same call later) or recoverable (`isRecoverable()`: call `stop()`, `configure()`, `start()`
again). Anything else means releasing the codec and creating a new one.

Common causes:
- The format, profile, or level is not supported by any decoder on the device. Query
  `MediaCodecList` and `MediaCodecInfo.CodecCapabilities` before configuring.
- Too many codec instances are alive at once. Hardware codecs are a shared, limited resource;
  release codecs you no longer use.
- The output `Surface` was released while the codec still used it.

Log the `diagnosticInfo` string from the exception; it names the failing component."}]}

messages.content: what's the right way to handle audio focus so playback pauses on an incoming call and resumes after? we request AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN but the transient loss case is inconsistent, do we need AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN_TRANSIENT and a separate resume in onAudioFocusChange?

content.text: I'll check the knowledge base on audio focus handling for calls.

input.query: audio focus incoming call AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN transient loss onAudioFocusChange resume

content.content:
{"results": [{"id": "audio-focus", "title": "Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)", "text": "# Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)

Android coordinates audio between apps with audio focus. An app that never requests focus,
or ignores focus loss, keeps playing over navigation prompts, calls, or other media.

Fix:
- With Media3, pass suitable `AudioAttributes` and `handleAudioFocus = true` to
  `ExoPlayer.setAudioAttributes(...)`; the player then requests focus, ducks, and pauses for you.
- Without Media3, request focus with an `AudioFocusRequest` (API 26+) and react to
  `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS`, `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT`, and `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT_CAN_DUCK`.
- Also handle `ACTION_AUDIO_BECOMING_NOISY` to pause when headphones are unplugged."}, {"id": "av-sync", "title": "Audio and video drift out of sync", "text": "# Audio and video drift out of sync

Players normally treat the audio clock as the master and schedule video frames against it.
Drift usually comes from wrong timestamps rather than from rendering speed.

Checks:
- Inspect stream start times and timestamps with `ffprobe -show_streams -show_frames`; a large
  `start_time` difference between audio and video streams shows up as constant offset.
- Variable-frame-rate recordings (common from phone cameras) can drift when a pipeline assumes
  a constant frame rate. Remux or transcode with correct timestamps.
- When writing a custom renderer, use `AudioTrack.getTimestamp()` to map audio frames to
  real time instead of counting written bytes."}, {"id": "mediacodec-errors", "title": "MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures", "text": "# MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures

`MediaCodec.CodecException` reports whether an error is transient (`isTransient()`: retry the
same call later) or recoverable (`isRecoverable()`: call `stop()`, `configure()`, `start()`
again). Anything else means releasing the codec and creating a new one.

Common causes:
- The format, profile, or level is not supported by any decoder on the device. Query
  `MediaCodecList` and `MediaCodecInfo.CodecCapabilities` before configuring.
- Too many codec instances are alive at once. Hardware codecs are a shared, limited resource;
  release codecs you no longer use.
- The output `Surface` was released while the codec still used it.

Log the `diagnosticInfo` string from the exception; it names the failing component."}]}

Likely cause: Probably not the gain type: the knowledge base says an app that ignores focus loss keeps playing over calls and tells you to react to AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS, AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT and AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT_CAN_DUCK, so the inconsistency is most likely in your onAudioFocusChange handling. Next step: In onAudioFocusChange, pause on AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT and remember that you paused for focus, resume only when AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN comes back and you paused it, and stop on AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS; or, with Media3, use setAudioAttributes(..., handleAudioFocus = true) so ExoPlayer requests focus and pauses for you.

Android ships a software AV1 decoder (`c2.android.av1.decoder`) starting with Android 10

devices on recent Android releases still decode AV1 in software only, which can be too slow
for high resolutions or frame rates.

{"results": [{"id": "behind-live-window", "title": "BehindLiveWindowException in Media3 / ExoPlayer live streams", "text": "# BehindLiveWindowException in Media3 / ExoPlayer live streams

A live stream exposes a sliding window of segments. If playback falls further behind than
the window (long pause, slow network, app in the background), the segments it needs are gone
and the player raises a `BehindLiveWindowException`, surfaced as a `PlaybackException` with
error code `ERROR_CODE_BEHIND_LIVE_WINDOW`.

Fix: in `Player.Listener.onPlayerError`, check for that error code, then call
`player.seekToDefaultPosition()` followed by `player.prepare()` to rejoin at the live edge.
Consider a longer live window on the server or a smaller target live offset on the client."}]}

content.text:
Likely cause: Your log shows "Caused by: androidx.media3.exoplayer.source.BehindLiveWindowException" and "onPlayerError code=1002 (ERROR_CODE_BEHIND_LIVE_WINDOW)": after the app was in the background the player fell behind the live window and the segments it needs are gone. The supported recovery is both steps together, not one or the other: call player.seekToDefaultPosition() and then player.prepare() to rejoin the live edge.
Next step: Do it in Player.Listener.onPlayerError, after checking for ERROR_CODE_BEHIND_LIVE_WINDOW, rather than in the activity resume callback; optionally also use a longer live window on the server or a smaller target live offset on the client.

input.query: AV1 decoder Android version older devices software decoder

content.content:
{"results": [{"id": "av1-decoding", "title": "AV1 decoding support on Android", "text": "# AV1 decoding support on Android

Android ships a software AV1 decoder (`c2.android.av1.decoder`) starting with Android 10
(API 29). Hardware AV1 decoding depends on the device's SoC, not on the Android version: many
devices on recent Android releases still decode AV1 in software only, which can be too slow
for high resolutions or frame rates.

Checks:
- Enumerate `MediaCodecList(MediaCodecList.REGULAR_CODECS)` for the MIME type `video/av01`.
- On API 29+, `MediaCodecInfo.isHardwareAccelerated()` tells you whether a decoder is
  hardware backed.
- Use `CodecCapabilities.getVideoCapabilities()` to check supported sizes and frame rates
  before choosing an AV1 rendition; fall back to VP9 or H.264/HEVC when needed."}, {"id": "audio-focus", "title": "Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)", "text": "# Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)

Android coordinates audio between apps with audio focus. An app that never requests focus,
or ignores focus loss, keeps playing over navigation prompts, calls, or other media.

Fix:
- With Media3, pass suitable `AudioAttributes` and `handleAudioFocus = true` to
  `ExoPlayer.setAudioAttributes(...)`; the player then requests focus, ducks, and pauses for you.
- Without Media3, request focus with an `AudioFocusRequest` (API 26+) and react to
  `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS`, `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT`, and `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT_CAN_DUCK`.
- Also handle `ACTION_AUDIO_BECOMING_NOISY` to pause when headphones are unplugged."}]}

messages.content: Some customers on a budget phone get SD even though the content is HD and the license is fine. How do we check which Widevine security level and max resolution the device reports, and how do we make the player request the highest rendition that device supports?

content.text: Let me check the knowledge base on Widevine levels and resolution caps.

input.query: Widevine security level L1 L3 max resolution MediaDrm

content.content:
{"results": [{"id": "widevine-levels", "title": "Widevine security levels and HD playback", "text": "# Widevine security levels and HD playback

Widevine has security levels: L1 (decryption and decoding inside a hardware trusted
environment) and L3 (software only). Content owners commonly restrict HD and higher
renditions to L1, so the same app may get only SD on an L3 device.

Checks:
- Read `MediaDrm(WIDEVINE_UUID).getPropertyString("securityLevel")`.
- A device can drop from L1 to L3 after an unlocked bootloader or a failed keybox
  provisioning; the license server then refuses HD keys.
- Log the license request and response status to tell a policy refusal apart from a
  network or provisioning error."}, {"id": "mediacodec-errors", "title": "MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures", "text": "# MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures

`MediaCodec.CodecException` reports whether an error is transient (`isTransient()`: retry the
same call later) or recoverable (`isRecoverable()`: call `stop()`, `configure()`, `start()`
again). Anything else means releasing the codec and creating a new one.

Common causes:
- The format, profile, or level is not supported by any decoder on the device. Query
  `MediaCodecList` and `MediaCodecInfo.CodecCapabilities` before configuring.
- Too many codec instances are alive at once. Hardware codecs are a shared, limited resource;
  release codecs you no longer use.
- The output `Surface` was released while the codec still used it.

Log the `diagnosticInfo` string from the exception; it names the failing component."}]}

function (PQ or HLG). When such a stream reaches a display path that is not HDR-capable and
nothing tone-maps it, colours look flat and grey or the picture looks far too dark.

devices on recent Android releases still decode AV1 in software only, which can be too slow
for high resolutions or frame rates.

content.content:
{"results": [{"id": "hdr-tone-mapping", "title": "HDR video looks washed out or too dark", "text": "# HDR video looks washed out or too dark

HDR10 and HLG streams carry a wide colour gamut (BT.2020) and a high-dynamic-range transfer
function (PQ or HLG). When such a stream reaches a display path that is not HDR-capable and
nothing tone-maps it, colours look flat and grey or the picture looks far too dark.

Checks:
- Ask the display what it supports: `Display.getHdrCapabilities()` (or `Display.isHdr()` on API 26+).
- Render to a `SurfaceView`. `TextureView` composites through the GPU and is a common reason
  HDR output gets flattened.
- Confirm the decoder output format reports the expected colour transfer
  (`MediaFormat.KEY_COLOR_TRANSFER`) and colour standard.
- If the display is SDR, tone-map explicitly (for example with a Media3 Transformer or
  effect pipeline) or serve an SDR rendition."}, {"id": "av1-decoding", "title": "AV1 decoding support on Android", "text": "# AV1 decoding support on Android

Android ships a software AV1 decoder (`c2.android.av1.decoder`) starting with Android 10
(API 29). Hardware AV1 decoding depends on the device's SoC, not on the Android version: many
devices on recent Android releases still decode AV1 in software only, which can be too slow
for high resolutions or frame rates.

Checks:
- Enumerate `MediaCodecList(MediaCodecList.REGULAR_CODECS)` for the MIME type `video/av01`.
- On API 29+, `MediaCodecInfo.isHardwareAccelerated()` tells you whether a decoder is
  hardware backed.
- Use `CodecCapabilities.getVideoCapabilities()` to check supported sizes and frame rates
  before choosing an AV1 rendition; fall back to VP9 or H.264/HEVC when needed."}]}

{"results": [{"id": "av-sync", "title": "Audio and video drift out of sync", "text": "# Audio and video drift out of sync

Players normally treat the audio clock as the master and schedule video frames against it.
Drift usually comes from wrong timestamps rather than from rendering speed.

Checks:
- Inspect stream start times and timestamps with `ffprobe -show_streams -show_frames`; a large
  `start_time` difference between audio and video streams shows up as constant offset.
- Variable-frame-rate recordings (common from phone cameras) can drift when a pipeline assumes
  a constant frame rate. Remux or transcode with correct timestamps.
- When writing a custom renderer, use `AudioTrack.getTimestamp()` to map audio frames to
  real time instead of counting written bytes."}, {"id": "hdr-tone-mapping", "title": "HDR video looks washed out or too dark", "text": "# HDR video looks washed out or too dark

HDR10 and HLG streams carry a wide colour gamut (BT.2020) and a high-dynamic-range transfer
function (PQ or HLG). When such a stream reaches a display path that is not HDR-capable and
nothing tone-maps it, colours look flat and grey or the picture looks far too dark.

Checks:
- Ask the display what it supports: `Display.getHdrCapabilities()` (or `Display.isHdr()` on API 26+).
- Render to a `SurfaceView`. `TextureView` composites through the GPU and is a common reason
  HDR output gets flattened.

  (`MediaFormat.KEY_COLOR_TRANSFER`) and colour standard.
- If the display is SDR, tone-map explicitly (for example with a Media3 Transformer or
  effect pipeline) or serve an SDR rendition."}, {"id": "audio-focus", "title": "Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)", "text": "# Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)

Android coordinates audio between apps with audio focus. An app that never requests focus,
or ignores focus loss, keeps playing over navigation prompts, calls, or other media.

Fix:
- With Media3, pass suitable `AudioAttributes` and `handleAudioFocus = true` to
  `ExoPlayer.setAudioAttributes(...)`; the player then requests focus, ducks, and pauses for you.

  `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS`, `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT`, and `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT_CAN_DUCK`.
- Also handle `ACTION_AUDIO_BECOMING_NOISY` to pause when headphones are unplugged."}]}

Android coordinates audio between apps with audio focus. An app that never requests focus,
or ignores focus loss, keeps playing over navigation prompts, calls, or other media.

Fix:
- With Media3, pass suitable `AudioAttributes` and `handleAudioFocus = true` to
  `ExoPlayer.setAudioAttributes(...)`; the player then requests focus, ducks, and pauses for you.
- Without Media3, request focus with an `AudioFocusRequest` (API 26+) and react to
  `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS`, `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT`, and `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT_CAN_DUCK`.
- Also handle `ACTION_AUDIO_BECOMING_NOISY` to pause when headphones are unplugged."}, {"id": "hdr-tone-mapping", "title": "HDR video looks washed out or too dark", "text": "# HDR video looks washed out or too dark

HDR10 and HLG streams carry a wide colour gamut (BT.2020) and a high-dynamic-range transfer
function (PQ or HLG). When such a stream reaches a display path that is not HDR-capable and
nothing tone-maps it, colours look flat and grey or the picture looks far too dark.

Checks:
- Ask the display what it supports: `Display.getHdrCapabilities()` (or `Display.isHdr()` on API 26+).
- Render to a `SurfaceView`. `TextureView` composites through the GPU and is a common reason
  HDR output gets flattened.

  (`MediaFormat.KEY_COLOR_TRANSFER`) and colour standard.

  effect pipeline) or serve an SDR rendition."}, {"id": "av1-decoding", "title": "AV1 decoding support on Android", "text": "# AV1 decoding support on Android

Android ships a software AV1 decoder (`c2.android.av1.decoder`) starting with Android 10
(API 29). Hardware AV1 decoding depends on the device's SoC, not on the Android version: many
devices on recent Android releases still decode AV1 in software only, which can be too slow
for high resolutions or frame rates.

Checks:
- Enumerate `MediaCodecList(MediaCodecList.REGULAR_CODECS)` for the MIME type `video/av01`.

A live stream exposes a sliding window of segments. If playback falls further behind than
the window (long pause, slow network, app in the background), the segments it needs are gone
and the player raises a `BehindLiveWindowException`, surfaced as a `PlaybackException` with
error code `ERROR_CODE_BEHIND_LIVE_WINDOW`.

Fix: in `Player.Listener.onPlayerError`, check for that error code, then call
`player.seekToDefaultPosition()` followed by `player.prepare()` to rejoin at the live edge.
Consider a longer live window on the server or a smaller target live offset on the client."}, {"id": "av-sync", "title": "Audio and video drift out of sync", "text": "# Audio and video drift out of sync

Players normally treat the audio clock as the master and schedule video frames against it.
Drift usually comes from wrong timestamps rather than from rendering speed.

Checks:
- Inspect stream start times and timestamps with `ffprobe -show_streams -show_frames`; a large
  `start_time` difference between audio and video streams shows up as constant offset.
- Variable-frame-rate recordings (common from phone cameras) can drift when a pipeline assumes
  a constant frame rate. Remux or transcode with correct timestamps.
- When writing a custom renderer, use `AudioTrack.getTimestamp()` to map audio frames to
  real time instead of counting written bytes."}]}

Players normally treat the audio clock as the master and schedule video frames against it.
Drift usually comes from wrong timestamps rather than from rendering speed.

  `start_time` difference between audio and video streams shows up as constant offset.

Android coordinates audio between apps with audio focus. An app that never requests focus,

- With Media3, pass suitable `AudioAttributes` and `handleAudioFocus = true` to
  `ExoPlayer.setAudioAttributes(...)`; the player then requests focus, ducks, and pauses for you.

  `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS`, `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT`, and `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT_CAN_DUCK`.

Players normally treat the audio clock as the master and schedule video frames against it.
Drift usually comes from wrong timestamps rather than from rendering speed.

Checks:
- Inspect stream start times and timestamps with `ffprobe -show_streams -show_frames`; a large
  `start_time` difference between audio and video streams shows up as constant offset.
- Variable-frame-rate recordings (common from phone cameras) can drift when a pipeline assumes
  a constant frame rate. Remux or transcode with correct timestamps.
- When writing a custom renderer, use `AudioTrack.getTimestamp()` to map audio frames to
  real time instead of counting written bytes."}, {"id": "audio-focus", "title": "Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)", "text": "# Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)

Android coordinates audio between apps with audio focus. An app that never requests focus,
or ignores focus loss, keeps playing over navigation prompts, calls, or other media.

Fix:
- With Media3, pass suitable `AudioAttributes` and `handleAudioFocus = true` to
  `ExoPlayer.setAudioAttributes(...)`; the player then requests focus, ducks, and pauses for you.
- Without Media3, request focus with an `AudioFocusRequest` (API 26+) and react to
  `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS`, `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT`, and `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT_CAN_DUCK`.
- Also handle `ACTION_AUDIO_BECOMING_NOISY` to pause when headphones are unplugged."}]}

{"results": [{"id": "hdr-tone-mapping", "title": "HDR video looks washed out or too dark", "text": "# HDR video looks washed out or too dark

HDR10 and HLG streams carry a wide colour gamut (BT.2020) and a high-dynamic-range transfer
function (PQ or HLG). When such a stream reaches a display path that is not HDR-capable and
nothing tone-maps it, colours look flat and grey or the picture looks far too dark.

Checks:
- Ask the display what it supports: `Display.getHdrCapabilities()` (or `Display.isHdr()` on API 26+).
- Render to a `SurfaceView`. `TextureView` composites through the GPU and is a common reason
  HDR output gets flattened.
- Confirm the decoder output format reports the expected colour transfer
  (`MediaFormat.KEY_COLOR_TRANSFER`) and colour standard.
- If the display is SDR, tone-map explicitly (for example with a Media3 Transformer or
  effect pipeline) or serve an SDR rendition."}, {"id": "widevine-levels", "title": "Widevine security levels and HD playback", "text": "# Widevine security levels and HD playback

Widevine has security levels: L1 (decryption and decoding inside a hardware trusted
environment) and L3 (software only). Content owners commonly restrict HD and higher
renditions to L1, so the same app may get only SD on an L3 device.

Checks:
- Read `MediaDrm(WIDEVINE_UUID).getPropertyString("securityLevel")`.
- A device can drop from L1 to L3 after an unlocked bootloader or a failed keybox
  provisioning; the license server then refuses HD keys.
- Log the license request and response status to tell a policy refusal apart from a
  network or provisioning error."}]}

messages.content: We need to check how our player handles audio focus when a call comes in. What's the right way to build an AudioFocusRequest with the correct AudioAttributes and handle AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT so playback pauses and resumes, and what should we test on a real device?

content.text: I'll check the knowledge base on audio focus handling for calls.

input.query: AudioFocusRequest AudioAttributes AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT pause resume phone call testing

content.content:
{"results": [{"id": "audio-focus", "title": "Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)", "text": "# Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)

Android coordinates audio between apps with audio focus. An app that never requests focus,
or ignores focus loss, keeps playing over navigation prompts, calls, or other media.

Fix:
- With Media3, pass suitable `AudioAttributes` and `handleAudioFocus = true` to
  `ExoPlayer.setAudioAttributes(...)`; the player then requests focus, ducks, and pauses for you.
- Without Media3, request focus with an `AudioFocusRequest` (API 26+) and react to
  `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS`, `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT`, and `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT_CAN_DUCK`.
- Also handle `ACTION_AUDIO_BECOMING_NOISY` to pause when headphones are unplugged."}, {"id": "behind-live-window", "title": "BehindLiveWindowException in Media3 / ExoPlayer live streams", "text": "# BehindLiveWindowException in Media3 / ExoPlayer live streams

A live stream exposes a sliding window of segments. If playback falls further behind than
the window (long pause, slow network, app in the background), the segments it needs are gone
and the player raises a `BehindLiveWindowException`, surfaced as a `PlaybackException` with
error code `ERROR_CODE_BEHIND_LIVE_WINDOW`.

Fix: in `Player.Listener.onPlayerError`, check for that error code, then call
`player.seekToDefaultPosition()` followed by `player.prepare()` to rejoin at the live edge.
Consider a longer live window on the server or a smaller target live offset on the client."}, {"id": "mediacodec-errors", "title": "MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures", "text": "# MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures

`MediaCodec.CodecException` reports whether an error is transient (`isTransient()`: retry the
same call later) or recoverable (`isRecoverable()`: call `stop()`, `configure()`, `start()`
again). Anything else means releasing the codec and creating a new one.

Common causes:
- The format, profile, or level is not supported by any decoder on the device. Query
  `MediaCodecList` and `MediaCodecInfo.CodecCapabilities` before configuring.
- Too many codec instances are alive at once. Hardware codecs are a shared, limited resource;
  release codecs you no longer use.
- The output `Surface` was released while the codec still used it.

Log the `diagnosticInfo` string from the exception; it names the failing component."}]}

content.text:
Likely cause: Per the knowledge base, an app that never requests focus or ignores focus loss keeps playing over calls, so the player must request focus with an AudioFocusRequest (API 26+) and react to AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS, AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT and AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT_CAN_DUCK. Build it with AudioFocusRequest.Builder(AudioManager.AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN), AudioAttributes of USAGE_MEDIA with a content type matching your media (CONTENT_TYPE_MUSIC or CONTENT_TYPE_MOVIE), and a setOnAudioFocusChangeListener that pauses on AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT (what an incoming call sends), resumes on AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN only if you paused it yourself, stops on AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS, and lowers volume on CAN_DUCK. (I did not run any device tool, so this is guidance rather than a diagnosis of your player.)
Next step: Test on a real device by playing, placing an incoming call, answering and hanging up (playback should pause, then resume), then repeat with the call declined, with a second media app taking focus (expect a permanent loss, no auto-resume), with a navigation prompt (duck), and with headphones unplugged (handle ACTION_AUDIO_BECOMING_NOISY); if you use Media3, ExoPlayer.setAudioAttributes(attrs, true) does the request, ducking and pausing for you.
Sources: [kb:audio-focus]

{"results": [{"id": "av1-decoding", "title": "AV1 decoding support on Android", "text": "# AV1 decoding support on Android

Android ships a software AV1 decoder (`c2.android.av1.decoder`) starting with Android 10
(API 29). Hardware AV1 decoding depends on the device's SoC, not on the Android version: many
devices on recent Android releases still decode AV1 in software only, which can be too slow
for high resolutions or frame rates.

Checks:
- Enumerate `MediaCodecList(MediaCodecList.REGULAR_CODECS)` for the MIME type `video/av01`.
- On API 29+, `MediaCodecInfo.isHardwareAccelerated()` tells you whether a decoder is
  hardware backed.
- Use `CodecCapabilities.getVideoCapabilities()` to check supported sizes and frame rates
  before choosing an AV1 rendition; fall back to VP9 or H.264/HEVC when needed."}, {"id": "mediacodec-errors", "title": "MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures", "text": "# MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures

`MediaCodec.CodecException` reports whether an error is transient (`isTransient()`: retry the
same call later) or recoverable (`isRecoverable()`: call `stop()`, `configure()`, `start()`
again). Anything else means releasing the codec and creating a new one.

Common causes:
- The format, profile, or level is not supported by any decoder on the device. Query
  `MediaCodecList` and `MediaCodecInfo.CodecCapabilities` before configuring.
- Too many codec instances are alive at once. Hardware codecs are a shared, limited resource;
  release codecs you no longer use.
- The output `Surface` was released while the codec still used it.

Log the `diagnosticInfo` string from the exception; it names the failing component."}]}

Android coordinates audio between apps with audio focus. An app that never requests focus,
or ignores focus loss, keeps playing over navigation prompts, calls, or other media.

Fix:
- With Media3, pass suitable `AudioAttributes` and `handleAudioFocus = true` to
  `ExoPlayer.setAudioAttributes(...)`; the player then requests focus, ducks, and pauses for you.
- Without Media3, request focus with an `AudioFocusRequest` (API 26+) and react to
  `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS`, `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT`, and `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT_CAN_DUCK`.
- Also handle `ACTION_AUDIO_BECOMING_NOISY` to pause when headphones are unplugged."}, {"id": "av-sync", "title": "Audio and video drift out of sync", "text": "# Audio and video drift out of sync

Players normally treat the audio clock as the master and schedule video frames against it.
Drift usually comes from wrong timestamps rather than from rendering speed.

Checks:
- Inspect stream start times and timestamps with `ffprobe -show_streams -show_frames`; a large
  `start_time` difference between audio and video streams shows up as constant offset.
- Variable-frame-rate recordings (common from phone cameras) can drift when a pipeline assumes
  a constant frame rate. Remux or transcode with correct timestamps.
- When writing a custom renderer, use `AudioTrack.getTimestamp()` to map audio frames to
  real time instead of counting written bytes."}, {"id": "behind-live-window", "title": "BehindLiveWindowException in Media3 / ExoPlayer live streams", "text": "# BehindLiveWindowException in Media3 / ExoPlayer live streams

A live stream exposes a sliding window of segments. If playback falls further behind than
the window (long pause, slow network, app in the background), the segments it needs are gone
and the player raises a `BehindLiveWindowException`, surfaced as a `PlaybackException` with
error code `ERROR_CODE_BEHIND_LIVE_WINDOW`.

Fix: in `Player.Listener.onPlayerError`, check for that error code, then call
`player.seekToDefaultPosition()` followed by `player.prepare()` to rejoin at the live edge.

content.content:
{"results": [{"id": "av1-decoding", "title": "AV1 decoding support on Android", "text": "# AV1 decoding support on Android

Android ships a software AV1 decoder (`c2.android.av1.decoder`) starting with Android 10
(API 29). Hardware AV1 decoding depends on the device's SoC, not on the Android version: many
devices on recent Android releases still decode AV1 in software only, which can be too slow
for high resolutions or frame rates.

Checks:
- Enumerate `MediaCodecList(MediaCodecList.REGULAR_CODECS)` for the MIME type `video/av01`.
- On API 29+, `MediaCodecInfo.isHardwareAccelerated()` tells you whether a decoder is
  hardware backed.
- Use `CodecCapabilities.getVideoCapabilities()` to check supported sizes and frame rates
  before choosing an AV1 rendition; fall back to VP9 or H.264/HEVC when needed."}, {"id": "mediacodec-errors", "title": "MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures", "text": "# MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures

`MediaCodec.CodecException` reports whether an error is transient (`isTransient()`: retry the
same call later) or recoverable (`isRecoverable()`: call `stop()`, `configure()`, `start()`
again). Anything else means releasing the codec and creating a new one.

Common causes:
- The format, profile, or level is not supported by any decoder on the device. Query
  `MediaCodecList` and `MediaCodecInfo.CodecCapabilities` before configuring.
- Too many codec instances are alive at once. Hardware codecs are a shared, limited resource;
  release codecs you no longer use.
- The output `Surface` was released while the codec still used it.

Log the `diagnosticInfo` string from the exception; it names the failing component."}, {"id": "widevine-levels", "title": "Widevine security levels and HD playback", "text": "# Widevine security levels and HD playback

Widevine has security levels: L1 (decryption and decoding inside a hardware trusted
environment) and L3 (software only). Content owners commonly restrict HD and higher
renditions to L1, so the same app may get only SD on an L3 device.

Checks:
- Read `MediaDrm(WIDEVINE_UUID).getPropertyString("securityLevel")`.
- A device can drop from L1 to L3 after an unlocked bootloader or a failed keybox
  provisioning; the license server then refuses HD keys.
- Log the license request and response status to tell a policy refusal apart from a
  network or provisioning error."}]}

{"results": [{"id": "widevine-levels", "title": "Widevine security levels and HD playback", "text": "# Widevine security levels and HD playback

Widevine has security levels: L1 (decryption and decoding inside a hardware trusted
environment) and L3 (software only). Content owners commonly restrict HD and higher
renditions to L1, so the same app may get only SD on an L3 device.

Checks:
- Read `MediaDrm(WIDEVINE_UUID).getPropertyString("securityLevel")`.
- A device can drop from L1 to L3 after an unlocked bootloader or a failed keybox
  provisioning; the license server then refuses HD keys.
- Log the license request and response status to tell a policy refusal apart from a
  network or provisioning error."}, {"id": "hdr-tone-mapping", "title": "HDR video looks washed out or too dark", "text": "# HDR video looks washed out or too dark

HDR10 and HLG streams carry a wide colour gamut (BT.2020) and a high-dynamic-range transfer
function (PQ or HLG). When such a stream reaches a display path that is not HDR-capable and
nothing tone-maps it, colours look flat and grey or the picture looks far too dark.

Checks:
- Ask the display what it supports: `Display.getHdrCapabilities()` (or `Display.isHdr()` on API 26+).
- Render to a `SurfaceView`. `TextureView` composites through the GPU and is a common reason
  HDR output gets flattened.
- Confirm the decoder output format reports the expected colour transfer
  (`MediaFormat.KEY_COLOR_TRANSFER`) and colour standard.
- If the display is SDR, tone-map explicitly (for example with a Media3 Transformer or
  effect pipeline) or serve an SDR rendition."}]}

{"results": [{"id": "av-sync", "title": "Audio and video drift out of sync", "text": "# Audio and video drift out of sync

Players normally treat the audio clock as the master and schedule video frames against it.
Drift usually comes from wrong timestamps rather than from rendering speed.

Checks:
- Inspect stream start times and timestamps with `ffprobe -show_streams -show_frames`; a large
  `start_time` difference between audio and video streams shows up as constant offset.
- Variable-frame-rate recordings (common from phone cameras) can drift when a pipeline assumes
  a constant frame rate. Remux or transcode with correct timestamps.
- When writing a custom renderer, use `AudioTrack.getTimestamp()` to map audio frames to
  real time instead of counting written bytes."}, {"id": "mp4-faststart", "title": "Progressive MP4 takes long to start (moov atom at the end)", "text": "# Progressive MP4 takes long to start (moov atom at the end)

An MP4 file's index (the `moov` atom) is often written at the end of the file by recorders and
encoders. A progressive-download player must then fetch the end of the file before playback can
begin, which shows up as a long start delay or extra range requests.

Checks and fix:
- `ffprobe -v trace file.mp4 2>&1 | grep -m2 -E "type:'(moov|mdat)'"` shows which atom comes first.
- Remux with the index at the front: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c copy -movflags +faststart out.mp4`.
- For adaptive streaming, prefer fragmented MP4 (DASH or HLS) instead."}, {"id": "audio-focus", "title": "Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)", "text": "# Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)

Android coordinates audio between apps with audio focus. An app that never requests focus,
or ignores focus loss, keeps playing over navigation prompts, calls, or other media.

Fix:
- With Media3, pass suitable `AudioAttributes` and `handleAudioFocus = true` to
  `ExoPlayer.setAudioAttributes(...)`; the player then requests focus, ducks, and pauses for you.

again). Anything else means releasing the codec and creating a new one.

Common causes:
- The format, profile, or level is not supported by any decoder on the device. Query
  `MediaCodecList` and `MediaCodecInfo.CodecCapabilities` before configuring.
- Too many codec instances are alive at once. Hardware codecs are a shared, limited resource;
  release codecs you no longer use.

Log the `diagnosticInfo` string from the exception; it names the failing component."}]}

{"results": [{"id": "mp4-faststart", "title": "Progressive MP4 takes long to start (moov atom at the end)", "text": "# Progressive MP4 takes long to start (moov atom at the end)

An MP4 file's index (the `moov` atom) is often written at the end of the file by recorders and
encoders. A progressive-download player must then fetch the end of the file before playback can
begin, which shows up as a long start delay or extra range requests.

Checks and fix:
- `ffprobe -v trace file.mp4 2>&1 | grep -m2 -E "type:'(moov|mdat)'"` shows which atom comes first.
- Remux with the index at the front: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c copy -movflags +faststart out.mp4`.
- For adaptive streaming, prefer fragmented MP4 (DASH or HLS) instead."}, {"id": "av-sync", "title": "Audio and video drift out of sync", "text": "# Audio and video drift out of sync

Players normally treat the audio clock as the master and schedule video frames against it.
Drift usually comes from wrong timestamps rather than from rendering speed.

Checks:
- Inspect stream start times and timestamps with `ffprobe -show_streams -show_frames`; a large
  `start_time` difference between audio and video streams shows up as constant offset.
- Variable-frame-rate recordings (common from phone cameras) can drift when a pipeline assumes
  a constant frame rate. Remux or transcode with correct timestamps.
- When writing a custom renderer, use `AudioTrack.getTimestamp()` to map audio frames to
  real time instead of counting written bytes."}, {"id": "audio-focus", "title": "Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)", "text": "# Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)

Android coordinates audio between apps with audio focus. An app that never requests focus,
or ignores focus loss, keeps playing over navigation prompts, calls, or other media.

Fix:
- With Media3, pass suitable `AudioAttributes` and `handleAudioFocus = true` to
  `ExoPlayer.setAudioAttributes(...)`; the player then requests focus, ducks, and pauses for you.
- Without Media3, request focus with an `AudioFocusRequest` (API 26+) and react to
  `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS`, `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT`, and `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT_CAN_DUCK`.
- Also handle `ACTION_AUDIO_BECOMING_NOISY` to pause when headphones are unplugged."}]}

encoders. A progressive-download player must then fetch the end of the file before playback can
begin, which shows up as a long start delay or extra range requests.

- `ffprobe -v trace file.mp4 2>&1 | grep -m2 -E "type:'(moov|mdat)'"` shows which atom comes first.

and the player raises a `BehindLiveWindowException`, surfaced as a `PlaybackException` with
error code `ERROR_CODE_BEHIND_LIVE_WINDOW`.

Fix: in `Player.Listener.onPlayerError`, check for that error code, then call
`player.seekToDefaultPosition()` followed by `player.prepare()` to rejoin at the live edge.

content.content:
{"results": [{"id": "widevine-levels", "title": "Widevine security levels and HD playback", "text": "# Widevine security levels and HD playback

Widevine has security levels: L1 (decryption and decoding inside a hardware trusted
environment) and L3 (software only). Content owners commonly restrict HD and higher
renditions to L1, so the same app may get only SD on an L3 device.

Checks:
- Read `MediaDrm(WIDEVINE_UUID).getPropertyString("securityLevel")`.
- A device can drop from L1 to L3 after an unlocked bootloader or a failed keybox
  provisioning; the license server then refuses HD keys.
- Log the license request and response status to tell a policy refusal apart from a
  network or provisioning error."}, {"id": "av-sync", "title": "Audio and video drift out of sync", "text": "# Audio and video drift out of sync

Players normally treat the audio clock as the master and schedule video frames against it.
Drift usually comes from wrong timestamps rather than from rendering speed.

Checks:
- Inspect stream start times and timestamps with `ffprobe -show_streams -show_frames`; a large
  `start_time` difference between audio and video streams shows up as constant offset.
- Variable-frame-rate recordings (common from phone cameras) can drift when a pipeline assumes
  a constant frame rate. Remux or transcode with correct timestamps.
- When writing a custom renderer, use `AudioTrack.getTimestamp()` to map audio frames to
  real time instead of counting written bytes."}, {"id": "behind-live-window", "title": "BehindLiveWindowException in Media3 / ExoPlayer live streams", "text": "# BehindLiveWindowException in Media3 / ExoPlayer live streams

A live stream exposes a sliding window of segments. If playback falls further behind than
the window (long pause, slow network, app in the background), the segments it needs are gone
and the player raises a `BehindLiveWindowException`, surfaced as a `PlaybackException` with
error code `ERROR_CODE_BEHIND_LIVE_WINDOW`.

Fix: in `Player.Listener.onPlayerError`, check for that error code, then call
`player.seekToDefaultPosition()` followed by `player.prepare()` to rejoin at the live edge.
Consider a longer live window on the server or a smaller target live offset on the client."}]}

content.content:
{"results": [{"id": "audio-focus", "title": "Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)", "text": "# Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)

Android coordinates audio between apps with audio focus. An app that never requests focus,
or ignores focus loss, keeps playing over navigation prompts, calls, or other media.

Fix:
- With Media3, pass suitable `AudioAttributes` and `handleAudioFocus = true` to
  `ExoPlayer.setAudioAttributes(...)`; the player then requests focus, ducks, and pauses for you.
- Without Media3, request focus with an `AudioFocusRequest` (API 26+) and react to
  `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS`, `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT`, and `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT_CAN_DUCK`.
- Also handle `ACTION_AUDIO_BECOMING_NOISY` to pause when headphones are unplugged."}, {"id": "av-sync", "title": "Audio and video drift out of sync", "text": "# Audio and video drift out of sync

Players normally treat the audio clock as the master and schedule video frames against it.
Drift usually comes from wrong timestamps rather than from rendering speed.

Checks:
- Inspect stream start times and timestamps with `ffprobe -show_streams -show_frames`; a large
  `start_time` difference between audio and video streams shows up as constant offset.
- Variable-frame-rate recordings (common from phone cameras) can drift when a pipeline assumes
  a constant frame rate. Remux or transcode with correct timestamps.
- When writing a custom renderer, use `AudioTrack.getTimestamp()` to map audio frames to
  real time instead of counting written bytes."}, {"id": "mediacodec-errors", "title": "MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures", "text": "# MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures

`MediaCodec.CodecException` reports whether an error is transient (`isTransient()`: retry the
same call later) or recoverable (`isRecoverable()`: call `stop()`, `configure()`, `start()`
again). Anything else means releasing the codec and creating a new one.

Common causes:
- The format, profile, or level is not supported by any decoder on the device. Query
  `MediaCodecList` and `MediaCodecInfo.CodecCapabilities` before configuring.
- Too many codec instances are alive at once. Hardware codecs are a shared, limited resource;
  release codecs you no longer use.
- The output `Surface` was released while the codec still used it.

Log the `diagnosticInfo` string from the exception; it names the failing component."}]}

{"results": [{"id": "mp4-faststart", "title": "Progressive MP4 takes long to start (moov atom at the end)", "text": "# Progressive MP4 takes long to start (moov atom at the end)

An MP4 file's index (the `moov` atom) is often written at the end of the file by recorders and
encoders. A progressive-download player must then fetch the end of the file before playback can
begin, which shows up as a long start delay or extra range requests.

Checks and fix:
- `ffprobe -v trace file.mp4 2>&1 | grep -m2 -E "type:'(moov|mdat)'"` shows which atom comes first.
- Remux with the index at the front: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c copy -movflags +faststart out.mp4`.
- For adaptive streaming, prefer fragmented MP4 (DASH or HLS) instead."}, {"id": "audio-focus", "title": "Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)", "text": "# Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)

Android coordinates audio between apps with audio focus. An app that never requests focus,
or ignores focus loss, keeps playing over navigation prompts, calls, or other media.

Fix:
- With Media3, pass suitable `AudioAttributes` and `handleAudioFocus = true` to
  `ExoPlayer.setAudioAttributes(...)`; the player then requests focus, ducks, and pauses for you.
- Without Media3, request focus with an `AudioFocusRequest` (API 26+) and react to
  `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS`, `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT`, and `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT_CAN_DUCK`.
- Also handle `ACTION_AUDIO_BECOMING_NOISY` to pause when headphones are unplugged."}]}

messages.content: HDR clips are coming out with flat grey colours on some phones. I think the tone mapping step is getting skipped but I'm not sure. What should I check first?

content.text: I'll check the knowledge base on HDR tone mapping and washed-out output.

input.query: HDR flat grey washed out tone mapping display HDR support

content.content:
{"results": [{"id": "hdr-tone-mapping", "title": "HDR video looks washed out or too dark", "text": "# HDR video looks washed out or too dark

HDR10 and HLG streams carry a wide colour gamut (BT.2020) and a high-dynamic-range transfer
function (PQ or HLG). When such a stream reaches a display path that is not HDR-capable and
nothing tone-maps it, colours look flat and grey or the picture looks far too dark.

Checks:
- Ask the display what it supports: `Display.getHdrCapabilities()` (or `Display.isHdr()` on API 26+).
- Render to a `SurfaceView`. `TextureView` composites through the GPU and is a common reason
  HDR output gets flattened.
- Confirm the decoder output format reports the expected colour transfer
  (`MediaFormat.KEY_COLOR_TRANSFER`) and colour standard.
- If the display is SDR, tone-map explicitly (for example with a Media3 Transformer or
  effect pipeline) or serve an SDR rendition."}, {"id": "av-sync", "title": "Audio and video drift out of sync", "text": "# Audio and video drift out of sync

Players normally treat the audio clock as the master and schedule video frames against it.
Drift usually comes from wrong timestamps rather than from rendering speed.

Checks:
- Inspect stream start times and timestamps with `ffprobe -show_streams -show_frames`; a large
  `start_time` difference between audio and video streams shows up as constant offset.
- Variable-frame-rate recordings (common from phone cameras) can drift when a pipeline assumes
  a constant frame rate. Remux or transcode with correct timestamps.
- When writing a custom renderer, use `AudioTrack.getTimestamp()` to map audio frames to
  real time instead of counting written bytes."}, {"id": "av1-decoding", "title": "AV1 decoding support on Android", "text": "# AV1 decoding support on Android

Android ships a software AV1 decoder (`c2.android.av1.decoder`) starting with Android 10
(API 29). Hardware AV1 decoding depends on the device's SoC, not on the Android version: many
devices on recent Android releases still decode AV1 in software only, which can be too slow
for high resolutions or frame rates.

Checks:
- Enumerate `MediaCodecList(MediaCodecList.REGULAR_CODECS)` for the MIME type `video/av01`.
- On API 29+, `MediaCodecInfo.isHardwareAccelerated()` tells you whether a decoder is
  hardware backed.
- Use `CodecCapabilities.getVideoCapabilities()` to check supported sizes and frame rates
  before choosing an AV1 rendition; fall back to VP9 or H.264/HEVC when needed."}]}

{"results": [{"id": "behind-live-window", "title": "BehindLiveWindowException in Media3 / ExoPlayer live streams", "text": "# BehindLiveWindowException in Media3 / ExoPlayer live streams

A live stream exposes a sliding window of segments. If playback falls further behind than
the window (long pause, slow network, app in the background), the segments it needs are gone
and the player raises a `BehindLiveWindowException`, surfaced as a `PlaybackException` with
error code `ERROR_CODE_BEHIND_LIVE_WINDOW`.

Fix: in `Player.Listener.onPlayerError`, check for that error code, then call
`player.seekToDefaultPosition()` followed by `player.prepare()` to rejoin at the live edge.
Consider a longer live window on the server or a smaller target live offset on the client."}, {"id": "av-sync", "title": "Audio and video drift out of sync", "text": "# Audio and video drift out of sync

Players normally treat the audio clock as the master and schedule video frames against it.
Drift usually comes from wrong timestamps rather than from rendering speed.

Checks:
- Inspect stream start times and timestamps with `ffprobe -show_streams -show_frames`; a large
  `start_time` difference between audio and video streams shows up as constant offset.
- Variable-frame-rate recordings (common from phone cameras) can drift when a pipeline assumes
  a constant frame rate. Remux or transcode with correct timestamps.
- When writing a custom renderer, use `AudioTrack.getTimestamp()` to map audio frames to
  real time instead of counting written bytes."}]}

messages.content: On a device in the field, Widevine appears to resolve to L3 and caps us at SD. Is there a supported runtime check for the DRM security level, such as the MediaDrm securityLevel property, and what should we expect to see on an L3 device before we request the license?

content.content:
{"results": [{"id": "widevine-levels", "title": "Widevine security levels and HD playback", "text": "# Widevine security levels and HD playback

Widevine has security levels: L1 (decryption and decoding inside a hardware trusted
environment) and L3 (software only). Content owners commonly restrict HD and higher
renditions to L1, so the same app may get only SD on an L3 device.

Checks:
- Read `MediaDrm(WIDEVINE_UUID).getPropertyString("securityLevel")`.
- A device can drop from L1 to L3 after an unlocked bootloader or a failed keybox
  provisioning; the license server then refuses HD keys.
- Log the license request and response status to tell a policy refusal apart from a
  network or provisioning error."}]}

11-21 09:26:40.240  9402  9402 E ExoPlayerImplInternal:   androidx.media3.exoplayer.ExoPlaybackException: Source error
11-21 09:26:40.240  9402  9402 E ExoPlayerImplInternal:       at androidx.media3.exoplayer.ExoPlayerImplInternal.handleIoException(ExoPlayerImplInternal.java)
11-21 09:26:40.240  9402  9402 E ExoPlayerImplInternal:   Caused by: androidx.media3.exoplayer.source.BehindLiveWindowException
11-21 09:26:40.241  9402  9402 E LivePlayer: onPlayerError code=1002 (ERROR_CODE_BEHIND_LIVE_WINDOW)

Is the correct recovery to re-prepare, or to seekToDefaultPosition on the live window and call prepare() again? Should this be handled in onPlayerError or when the activity resumes?

content.text: I'll check the knowledge base on recovering from this error.

input.query: BehindLiveWindowException recovery seekToDefaultPosition prepare live window

content.content:
{"results": [{"id": "behind-live-window", "title": "BehindLiveWindowException in Media3 / ExoPlayer live streams", "text": "# BehindLiveWindowException in Media3 / ExoPlayer live streams

A live stream exposes a sliding window of segments. If playback falls further behind than
the window (long pause, slow network, app in the background), the segments it needs are gone
and the player raises a `BehindLiveWindowException`, surfaced as a `PlaybackException` with
error code `ERROR_CODE_BEHIND_LIVE_WINDOW`.

Fix: in `Player.Listener.onPlayerError`, check for that error code, then call
`player.seekToDefaultPosition()` followed by `player.prepare()` to rejoin at the live edge.
Consider a longer live window on the server or a smaller target live offset on the client."}]}

content.content: {"bit_rate": 621572, "duration_s": 2.0, "file": "av_offset_300ms.mp4", "format": "mov,mp4,m4a,3gp,3g2,mj2", "mp4_top_level_boxes": ["ftyp", "free", "mdat", "moov"], "streams": [{"avg_frame_rate": "30/1", "codec_name": "h264", "codec_type": "video", "height": 720, "index": 0, "pix_fmt": "yuv420p", "profile": "High", "start_time": "0.300000", "width": 1280}, {"channels": 1, "codec_name": "aac", "codec_type": "audio", "index": 1, "profile": "LC", "sample_rate": "48000", "start_time": "0.000000"}]}

{"results": [{"id": "av-sync", "title": "Audio and video drift out of sync", "text": "# Audio and video drift out of sync

Players normally treat the audio clock as the master and schedule video frames against it.
Drift usually comes from wrong timestamps rather than from rendering speed.

Checks:
- Inspect stream start times and timestamps with `ffprobe -show_streams -show_frames`; a large
  `start_time` difference between audio and video streams shows up as constant offset.
- Variable-frame-rate recordings (common from phone cameras) can drift when a pipeline assumes
  a constant frame rate. Remux or transcode with correct timestamps.
- When writing a custom renderer, use `AudioTrack.getTimestamp()` to map audio frames to
  real time instead of counting written bytes."}, {"id": "audio-focus", "title": "Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)", "text": "# Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)

Android coordinates audio between apps with audio focus. An app that never requests focus,
or ignores focus loss, keeps playing over navigation prompts, calls, or other media.

Fix:
- With Media3, pass suitable `AudioAttributes` and `handleAudioFocus = true` to
  `ExoPlayer.setAudioAttributes(...)`; the player then requests focus, ducks, and pauses for you.
- Without Media3, request focus with an `AudioFocusRequest` (API 26+) and react to
  `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS`, `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT`, and `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT_CAN_DUCK`.
- Also handle `ACTION_AUDIO_BECOMING_NOISY` to pause when headphones are unplugged."}]}

messages.content: HDR10 content looks washed out in our player on some phones but plays fine in the system gallery. we set the surface with default color settings. what should we check first to tell whether it's the player or the display path?

content.text: I'll check the knowledge base on HDR10 surface and display handling first.

input.query: HDR10 washed out default surface color settings display HDR support

content.content:
{"results": [{"id": "hdr-tone-mapping", "title": "HDR video looks washed out or too dark", "text": "# HDR video looks washed out or too dark

HDR10 and HLG streams carry a wide colour gamut (BT.2020) and a high-dynamic-range transfer
function (PQ or HLG). When such a stream reaches a display path that is not HDR-capable and
nothing tone-maps it, colours look flat and grey or the picture looks far too dark.

Checks:
- Ask the display what it supports: `Display.getHdrCapabilities()` (or `Display.isHdr()` on API 26+).
- Render to a `SurfaceView`. `TextureView` composites through the GPU and is a common reason
  HDR output gets flattened.
- Confirm the decoder output format reports the expected colour transfer
  (`MediaFormat.KEY_COLOR_TRANSFER`) and colour standard.
- If the display is SDR, tone-map explicitly (for example with a Media3 Transformer or
  effect pipeline) or serve an SDR rendition."}, {"id": "av-sync", "title": "Audio and video drift out of sync", "text": "# Audio and video drift out of sync

Players normally treat the audio clock as the master and schedule video frames against it.
Drift usually comes from wrong timestamps rather than from rendering speed.

Checks:
- Inspect stream start times and timestamps with `ffprobe -show_streams -show_frames`; a large
  `start_time` difference between audio and video streams shows up as constant offset.
- Variable-frame-rate recordings (common from phone cameras) can drift when a pipeline assumes
  a constant frame rate. Remux or transcode with correct timestamps.
- When writing a custom renderer, use `AudioTrack.getTimestamp()` to map audio frames to
  real time instead of counting written bytes."}, {"id": "av1-decoding", "title": "AV1 decoding support on Android", "text": "# AV1 decoding support on Android

Android ships a software AV1 decoder (`c2.android.av1.decoder`) starting with Android 10
(API 29). Hardware AV1 decoding depends on the device's SoC, not on the Android version: many
devices on recent Android releases still decode AV1 in software only, which can be too slow
for high resolutions or frame rates.

Checks:
- Enumerate `MediaCodecList(MediaCodecList.REGULAR_CODECS)` for the MIME type `video/av01`.
- On API 29+, `MediaCodecInfo.isHardwareAccelerated()` tells you whether a decoder is
  hardware backed.
- Use `CodecCapabilities.getVideoCapabilities()` to check supported sizes and frame rates
  before choosing an AV1 rendition; fall back to VP9 or H.264/HEVC when needed."}]}

messages.content: Since Android has shipped an AV1 decoder since Android 8, we can drop the software fallback for AV1 on our build. How should we check the codec list at runtime to choose between the hardware AV1 decoder and the software one, and is there a reason to keep a fallback?

input.query: AV1 decoder Android version hardware software fallback MediaCodecList

content.content:
{"results": [{"id": "av1-decoding", "title": "AV1 decoding support on Android", "text": "# AV1 decoding support on Android

Android ships a software AV1 decoder (`c2.android.av1.decoder`) starting with Android 10
(API 29). Hardware AV1 decoding depends on the device's SoC, not on the Android version: many
devices on recent Android releases still decode AV1 in software only, which can be too slow
for high resolutions or frame rates.

Checks:
- Enumerate `MediaCodecList(MediaCodecList.REGULAR_CODECS)` for the MIME type `video/av01`.
- On API 29+, `MediaCodecInfo.isHardwareAccelerated()` tells you whether a decoder is
  hardware backed.
- Use `CodecCapabilities.getVideoCapabilities()` to check supported sizes and frame rates
  before choosing an AV1 rendition; fall back to VP9 or H.264/HEVC when needed."}, {"id": "mediacodec-errors", "title": "MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures", "text": "# MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures

`MediaCodec.CodecException` reports whether an error is transient (`isTransient()`: retry the
same call later) or recoverable (`isRecoverable()`: call `stop()`, `configure()`, `start()`
again). Anything else means releasing the codec and creating a new one.

Common causes:
- The format, profile, or level is not supported by any decoder on the device. Query
  `MediaCodecList` and `MediaCodecInfo.CodecCapabilities` before configuring.
- Too many codec instances are alive at once. Hardware codecs are a shared, limited resource;
  release codecs you no longer use.
- The output `Surface` was released while the codec still used it.

Log the `diagnosticInfo` string from the exception; it names the failing component."}]}

content.content:
{"results": [{"id": "mp4-faststart", "title": "Progressive MP4 takes long to start (moov atom at the end)", "text": "# Progressive MP4 takes long to start (moov atom at the end)

An MP4 file's index (the `moov` atom) is often written at the end of the file by recorders and
encoders. A progressive-download player must then fetch the end of the file before playback can
begin, which shows up as a long start delay or extra range requests.

Checks and fix:
- `ffprobe -v trace file.mp4 2>&1 | grep -m2 -E "type:'(moov|mdat)'"` shows which atom comes first.
- Remux with the index at the front: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c copy -movflags +faststart out.mp4`.
- For adaptive streaming, prefer fragmented MP4 (DASH or HLS) instead."}, {"id": "av1-decoding", "title": "AV1 decoding support on Android", "text": "# AV1 decoding support on Android

Android ships a software AV1 decoder (`c2.android.av1.decoder`) starting with Android 10
(API 29). Hardware AV1 decoding depends on the device's SoC, not on the Android version: many
devices on recent Android releases still decode AV1 in software only, which can be too slow
for high resolutions or frame rates.

Checks:
- Enumerate `MediaCodecList(MediaCodecList.REGULAR_CODECS)` for the MIME type `video/av01`.
- On API 29+, `MediaCodecInfo.isHardwareAccelerated()` tells you whether a decoder is
  hardware backed.
- Use `CodecCapabilities.getVideoCapabilities()` to check supported sizes and frame rates
  before choosing an AV1 rendition; fall back to VP9 or H.264/HEVC when needed."}]}

Fix:
- With Media3, pass suitable `AudioAttributes` and `handleAudioFocus = true` to
  `ExoPlayer.setAudioAttributes(...)`; the player then requests focus, ducks, and pauses for you.

again). Anything else means releasing the codec and creating a new one.

Common causes:
- The format, profile, or level is not supported by any decoder on the device. Query
  `MediaCodecList` and `MediaCodecInfo.CodecCapabilities` before configuring.
- Too many codec instances are alive at once. Hardware codecs are a shared, limited resource;
  release codecs you no longer use.

content.content:
{"results": [{"id": "av1-decoding", "title": "AV1 decoding support on Android", "text": "# AV1 decoding support on Android

Android ships a software AV1 decoder (`c2.android.av1.decoder`) starting with Android 10
(API 29). Hardware AV1 decoding depends on the device's SoC, not on the Android version: many
devices on recent Android releases still decode AV1 in software only, which can be too slow
for high resolutions or frame rates.

Checks:
- Enumerate `MediaCodecList(MediaCodecList.REGULAR_CODECS)` for the MIME type `video/av01`.
- On API 29+, `MediaCodecInfo.isHardwareAccelerated()` tells you whether a decoder is
  hardware backed.
- Use `CodecCapabilities.getVideoCapabilities()` to check supported sizes and frame rates
  before choosing an AV1 rendition; fall back to VP9 or H.264/HEVC when needed."}, {"id": "mediacodec-errors", "title": "MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures", "text": "# MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures

`MediaCodec.CodecException` reports whether an error is transient (`isTransient()`: retry the
same call later) or recoverable (`isRecoverable()`: call `stop()`, `configure()`, `start()`
again). Anything else means releasing the codec and creating a new one.

Common causes:
- The format, profile, or level is not supported by any decoder on the device. Query
  `MediaCodecList` and `MediaCodecInfo.CodecCapabilities` before configuring.
- Too many codec instances are alive at once. Hardware codecs are a shared, limited resource;
  release codecs you no longer use.
- The output `Surface` was released while the codec still used it.

Log the `diagnosticInfo` string from the exception; it names the failing component."}, {"id": "audio-focus", "title": "Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)", "text": "# Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)

Android coordinates audio between apps with audio focus. An app that never requests focus,
or ignores focus loss, keeps playing over navigation prompts, calls, or other media.

Fix:
- With Media3, pass suitable `AudioAttributes` and `handleAudioFocus = true` to
  `ExoPlayer.setAudioAttributes(...)`; the player then requests focus, ducks, and pauses for you.
- Without Media3, request focus with an `AudioFocusRequest` (API 26+) and react to
  `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS`, `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT`, and `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT_CAN_DUCK`.
- Also handle `ACTION_AUDIO_BECOMING_NOISY` to pause when headphones are unplugged."}]}

Android coordinates audio between apps with audio focus. An app that never requests focus,
or ignores focus loss, keeps playing over navigation prompts, calls, or other media.

Fix:
- With Media3, pass suitable `AudioAttributes` and `handleAudioFocus = true` to
  `ExoPlayer.setAudioAttributes(...)`; the player then requests focus, ducks, and pauses for you.
- Without Media3, request focus with an `AudioFocusRequest` (API 26+) and react to
  `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS`, `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT`, and `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT_CAN_DUCK`.
- Also handle `ACTION_AUDIO_BECOMING_NOISY` to pause when headphones are unplugged."}, {"id": "av-sync", "title": "Audio and video drift out of sync", "text": "# Audio and video drift out of sync

Players normally treat the audio clock as the master and schedule video frames against it.
Drift usually comes from wrong timestamps rather than from rendering speed.

Checks:
- Inspect stream start times and timestamps with `ffprobe -show_streams -show_frames`; a large
  `start_time` difference between audio and video streams shows up as constant offset.
- Variable-frame-rate recordings (common from phone cameras) can drift when a pipeline assumes
  a constant frame rate. Remux or transcode with correct timestamps.
- When writing a custom renderer, use `AudioTrack.getTimestamp()` to map audio frames to
  real time instead of counting written bytes."}, {"id": "behind-live-window", "title": "BehindLiveWindowException in Media3 / ExoPlayer live streams", "text": "# BehindLiveWindowException in Media3 / ExoPlayer live streams

A live stream exposes a sliding window of segments. If playback falls further behind than
the window (long pause, slow network, app in the background), the segments it needs are gone
and the player raises a `BehindLiveWindowException`, surfaced as a `PlaybackException` with
error code `ERROR_CODE_BEHIND_LIVE_WINDOW`.

Fix: in `Player.Listener.onPlayerError`, check for that error code, then call
`player.seekToDefaultPosition()` followed by `player.prepare()` to rejoin at the live edge.
Consider a longer live window on the server or a smaller target live offset on the client."}]}

{"results": [{"id": "mp4-faststart", "title": "Progressive MP4 takes long to start (moov atom at the end)", "text": "# Progressive MP4 takes long to start (moov atom at the end)

An MP4 file's index (the `moov` atom) is often written at the end of the file by recorders and
encoders. A progressive-download player must then fetch the end of the file before playback can
begin, which shows up as a long start delay or extra range requests.

Checks and fix:
- `ffprobe -v trace file.mp4 2>&1 | grep -m2 -E "type:'(moov|mdat)'"` shows which atom comes first.
- Remux with the index at the front: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c copy -movflags +faststart out.mp4`.
- For adaptive streaming, prefer fragmented MP4 (DASH or HLS) instead."}, {"id": "av1-decoding", "title": "AV1 decoding support on Android", "text": "# AV1 decoding support on Android

Android ships a software AV1 decoder (`c2.android.av1.decoder`) starting with Android 10
(API 29). Hardware AV1 decoding depends on the device's SoC, not on the Android version: many
devices on recent Android releases still decode AV1 in software only, which can be too slow
for high resolutions or frame rates.

Checks:
- Enumerate `MediaCodecList(MediaCodecList.REGULAR_CODECS)` for the MIME type `video/av01`.
- On API 29+, `MediaCodecInfo.isHardwareAccelerated()` tells you whether a decoder is
  hardware backed.
- Use `CodecCapabilities.getVideoCapabilities()` to check supported sizes and frame rates
  before choosing an AV1 rendition; fall back to VP9 or H.264/HEVC when needed."}]}

messages.content: music in our app keeps playing over phone calls ringing sometimes but not always. dont know why, were just the player. what would cause that and what do we need to check

content.text: I'll check the knowledge base on audio focus and phone calls.

input.query: audio focus phone call ringing music keeps playing requestAudioFocus

content.content:
{"results": [{"id": "audio-focus", "title": "Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)", "text": "# Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)

Android coordinates audio between apps with audio focus. An app that never requests focus,
or ignores focus loss, keeps playing over navigation prompts, calls, or other media.

Fix:
- With Media3, pass suitable `AudioAttributes` and `handleAudioFocus = true` to
  `ExoPlayer.setAudioAttributes(...)`; the player then requests focus, ducks, and pauses for you.
- Without Media3, request focus with an `AudioFocusRequest` (API 26+) and react to
  `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS`, `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT`, and `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT_CAN_DUCK`.
- Also handle `ACTION_AUDIO_BECOMING_NOISY` to pause when headphones are unplugged."}, {"id": "av-sync", "title": "Audio and video drift out of sync", "text": "# Audio and video drift out of sync

Players normally treat the audio clock as the master and schedule video frames against it.
Drift usually comes from wrong timestamps rather than from rendering speed.

Checks:
- Inspect stream start times and timestamps with `ffprobe -show_streams -show_frames`; a large
  `start_time` difference between audio and video streams shows up as constant offset.
- Variable-frame-rate recordings (common from phone cameras) can drift when a pipeline assumes
  a constant frame rate. Remux or transcode with correct timestamps.
- When writing a custom renderer, use `AudioTrack.getTimestamp()` to map audio frames to
  real time instead of counting written bytes."}, {"id": "behind-live-window", "title": "BehindLiveWindowException in Media3 / ExoPlayer live streams", "text": "# BehindLiveWindowException in Media3 / ExoPlayer live streams

A live stream exposes a sliding window of segments. If playback falls further behind than
the window (long pause, slow network, app in the background), the segments it needs are gone
and the player raises a `BehindLiveWindowException`, surfaced as a `PlaybackException` with
error code `ERROR_CODE_BEHIND_LIVE_WINDOW`.

Fix: in `Player.Listener.onPlayerError`, check for that error code, then call
`player.seekToDefaultPosition()` followed by `player.prepare()` to rejoin at the live edge.
Consider a longer live window on the server or a smaller target live offset on the client."}]}
